summary: Reviewer consensus across CarExpert, CarsGuide and EV Central is that the BMW i4 eDrive35 remains genuinely engaging and comfortable to drive, even as BMW pared the local range back to this single grade for 2026, dropping the eDrive40 and M50 and readying the model for replacement by the Neue Klasse i3. CarsGuide scored the driving experience 10/10, but reviewers consistently flag pricing that undercuts few direct rivals, real-world range well short of the claimed figure, and cabin materials that feel a step below what BMW buyers expect. CarExpert's overall verdict of "Good" reflects a competent EV being overtaken by newer rivals on range and technology.
pros: Engaging, car-like driving dynamics with precise steering and confident handling praised across reviews
Comfortable, well-damped ride and a notably quiet, refined cabin at speed
Strong multimedia system with 12.3-inch digital cluster and 14.9-inch curved touchscreen
Fast DC charging (180kW, 32 minutes 10-80%) and now standard M Sport styling
cons: Real-world range (reviewers observed roughly 370km) falls well short of the claimed 448km
Expensive for what it offers, undercutting few direct rivals despite being the sole remaining variant
Interior materials feel plasticky and lack the polish reviewers expect of a BMW
Shorter warranty than some rivals, and the model is being phased out ahead of the incoming i3

summary: Australian reviewers rate the iX1 as one of the best small electric SUVs on sale, praising BMW's typically composed ride and precise steering alongside a genuinely upscale, well-finished cabin with quality materials and slick infotainment. It carries a clear price premium over mainstream EV rivals, and its roughly 400-450km real-world range trails segment leaders like the Tesla Model Y, but reviewers feel the driving experience and interior finish justify the extra spend for buyers prioritising refinement and brand prestige over outright value. CarExpert has named it its Best EV Small SUV in consecutive years, reflecting a broad consensus that BMW has successfully electrified its smallest SUV.
pros: Composed, well-damped ride and precise steering that reviewers say outclasses cheaper EV rivals
Upscale, well-finished interior with quality materials and an intuitive, slick infotainment system
Surprisingly spacious cabin for a compact SUV, with rear seat space rivalling the front
Back-to-back CarExpert Choice Award winner for Best EV Small SUV
cons: Premium pricing sits well above mainstream small EV SUVs and undercuts few direct rivals
Real-world range (reviewers report high-17s to high-18s kWh/100km) trails key rivals such as the Tesla Model Y
490L boot is smaller than the petrol X1's due to the rear-mounted motor and battery pack
Expensive scheduled servicing over a typical ownership period

summary: Sharply priced small SUV from BYD with a well-equipped cabin and a strong warranty, aimed squarely at first-time EV buyers.
pros: Cheapest list price in this comparison at $39,990 before on-road costs
6-year/150,000km warranty with BYD's LFP Blade battery chemistry
Quirky but well-finished interior with a rotating touchscreen and good standard equipment
cons: Shortest range of the three at 345km WLTP on the entry Essential variant
Smallest boot of the comparison at 440L seats up
Resale value in Australia is still largely unproven for the brand

summary: Australia's cheapest new electric car, the Dolphin pairs a soft, comfortable ride with a surprisingly well-equipped, upscale-feeling cabin for the price, according to CarExpert, CarsGuide and WhichCar. Reviewers agree it is happiest as a city runabout: refined and efficient around town, but wind noise, mixed rear visibility and (on the base Essential) modest power blunt its appeal on the open road. It is not a driver's car, but on value and everyday livability it comfortably outpoints most petrol light hatches at a similar price.
pros: Lowest entry price of any new EV in Australia
Comfortable, well-controlled ride for the segment
Roomy cabin and quality-feeling trim materials for the price
Strong standard equipment including a large rotating touchscreen
Five-star ANCAP safety rating with comprehensive driver assist tech
cons: Underpowered Essential struggles with highway overtaking
Slow 7kW AC home charging versus rivals' 11kW
Small boot and restricted rear visibility
6-year/150,000km warranty trails some rivals' 7-year cover
Steeper resale depreciation risk as BYD repeatedly cuts new prices

summary: The BYD Seal is a fast-charging, long-range electric sedan that undercuts the Tesla Model 3 on price while matching it on performance, especially in dual-motor Performance guise. Australian reviewers rate the equipment list, warranty and everyday value highly, but consistently flag a boot smaller than key rivals, an unsettled ride on rougher roads, and a touchscreen-heavy interior with few physical controls. Repeated BYD price cuts have also softened resale values across the range, a factor increasingly raised by reviewers and even BYD's own local distributor.
pros: Strong value against the Tesla Model 3, with a well-equipped cabin and quick acceleration in Performance guise (390kW/670Nm, 0-100km/h in 3.8s)
Long WLTP range from the 82.56kWh Blade LFP battery: 570km (Premium) and 520km (Performance), with 150kW DC fast charging
Strong after-sales backing with a 6-year/150,000km vehicle warranty and 8-year/160,000km battery warranty
cons: 400L boot trails key rivals like the Tesla Model 3 (594L) and Toyota Camry (524L), with a narrow opening
Ride quality criticised as unsettled and bouncy over bumps, lacking the composure of segment rivals
Interior tech feels dated relative to newer BYD models, with too many functions buried in touchscreen menus rather than physical controls
Reviewers and BYD's own Australian distributor have flagged softening resale values as BYD continues to cut new-car prices across its range

summary: Australian reviewers largely agree the Sealion 7 is one of the most convincing mainstream electric SUVs yet from a Chinese brand, praising its spacious, well-finished cabin, strong value against the Tesla Model Y, and a confident five-star ANCAP safety rating. The dual-motor Performance adds genuinely quick acceleration while keeping the comfortable, easy-to-live-with character of the range. Verdicts are more mixed on dynamics, with several outlets noting body roll, a ride that can feel soggy on the open road and jiggly around town, and lingering infotainment glitches.
pros: Spacious, well-finished cabin with generous rear-seat room and dual driver displays
Strong value against the Tesla Model Y, undercutting it while matching much of its specification
Five-star ANCAP safety rating (2025) with comprehensive standard driver-assist tech
Performance variant adds genuine pace (4.5s 0-100km/h) without losing everyday comfort
cons: Noticeable body roll and a ride that reviewers describe as soggy at speed and jiggly around town
Some tech gremlins and infotainment software glitches reported in early ownership
Real-world range and efficiency trail the claimed WLTP figures by a noticeable margin
BYD's Australian resale value and dealer/service network are still relatively unproven for the brand

summary: The Chery E5 (rebranded from Omoda E5 during 2025, with the Omoda name now being reserved for a separate model line launching later) is one of the cheapest new electric SUVs on sale in Australia, a small front-wheel-drive EV pitched squarely on price and standard equipment rather than dynamic polish. Australian reviewers consistently praise its value proposition, long warranty and cheap servicing, well-equipped cabin, but mark it down for unsettled ride quality, an over-cautious safety-assist calibration, and a boot that trails class rivals. For MY26 the range was simplified to a single Ultimate grade with a smaller but more efficient battery, holding range steady at 430km WLTP while sharpening the price further.
pros: One of the cheapest new electric SUVs on sale in Australia, undercutting most EV rivals
Long ownership package: 7-year vehicle / 8-year battery warranty plus affordable capped-price servicing (around $227/visit)
Well-equipped cabin for the price, with dual 12.3-inch screens, wireless charging and soft-touch trim
Solid 430km WLTP range from a modest, efficient battery
cons: Ride quality criticised as jittery and easily upset by rough surfaces around town, with some testers also describing wallowy handling at speed
Safety-assist calibration is poor: abrupt lane-keep intervention and over-sensitive driver-attention warnings that reviewers end up disabling
Small 300-litre boot (seats up) trails rivals offering closer to 450 litres
Slower DC fast-charging (around 80kW max) than newer rivals in the segment

summary: The EX5 is Geely's first model for the Australian market, a mid-size front-wheel-drive electric SUV pitched on comfort and value below better-known rivals like the Tesla Model Y. Reviewers consistently praise its quiet, cushioned ride and roomy, lounge-like rear seating, but mark it down for a smaller-than-expected boot, touchscreen-only climate controls, and driving dynamics that favour softness over sharpness. A mid-2026 update brought a larger 68.39kWh battery lifting range to 475km (Complete) and 450km (Inspire), addressing the main complaint about the original 2025 launch cars.
pros: Comfortable, well-cushioned ride tuned for Australian roads
Quiet cabin with strong urban energy efficiency
Sharp pricing relative to rivals such as Leapmotor C10 and Tesla Model Y
Spacious, lounge-like rear seat comfort
Long 7-year vehicle / 8-year battery warranty
cons: Boot space (302-410L) trails key rivals like the Leapmotor C10 (581L)
Modest ~100kW DC fast-charging rate
Touchscreen-only controls for climate and headlights are fiddly
No official towing rating in Australia as at mid-2026
Noticeable body roll and 'floaty' suspension feel when driven briskly

summary: Australian reviewers consistently praise the Inster's cleverly packaged, unexpectedly roomy cabin and its agile, fun-to-drive character in city conditions, with several noting it feels bigger inside than its tiny footprint suggests. The main point of criticism across CarsGuide, Zecar and Carscoops is value: at its current pricing the Inster sits noticeably above key budget-EV rivals like the BYD Dolphin and GWM Ora, undercutting its case as an affordable city runabout. Interior plastics are widely described as hard and budget-grade, and the rear bench is limited to two occupants rather than three.
pros: Cleverly packaged, surprisingly spacious cabin for such a small footprint, helped by sliding and fully-folding rear seats
Agile, easy-to-park city manners with light, precise steering
Distinctive, likeable styling that reviewers describe as fun and characterful
Extended Range and Cross variants add usefully more range and ground clearance over the entry Standard Range
cons: Priced noticeably higher than key budget-EV rivals such as the BYD Dolphin and GWM Ora, undermining its value case
Rear seating limited to four occupants in total, with only two rear seatbelts rather than three
Hard, budget-feeling interior plastics and no wireless Apple CarPlay/Android Auto
Standard Range's real-world range is modest for anything beyond city and inner-suburban driving

summary: Australian reviewers consistently rate the Ioniq 5 as one of the most complete mid-size electric SUVs on sale, praising its distinctive retro-futuristic styling, spacious and flexible cabin, and quick 800V DC charging. Ride comfort has improved with recent updates and is composed around town, though some testers still find body control loosens up over undulating country roads. The Ioniq 5 N adds genuine sports-car pace and track ability while retaining the practicality of the donor SUV, making it a standout among performance EVs, albeit at a steep price premium.
pros: Distinctive, spacious interior with a flat floor and sliding rear seats
Fast 800V charging architecture supports rapid top-ups on road trips
Comfortable, grown-up highway ride with low wind and tyre noise
Ioniq 5 N offers genuine performance-car dynamics in a practical SUV body
cons: Body control can feel loose and float-y over undulating roads at speed
Real-world efficiency trails some rivals, particularly on the AWD and N variants
Boot space is only average for the class
N Line Premium and N variants push well into luxury-car pricing territory

summary: Australian reviewers see the Kona Electric as a competent, easy-to-live-with small SUV with genuinely spacious packaging and a comfortable, relaxed ride around town, backed by Hyundai's dealer network. The Extended Range base grade is widely rated the pick of the range as strong value, while the Standard Range's real-world range and slow 100kW charging are seen as behind newer rivals, and the step up to Premium is questioned as not clearly worth the extra outlay. Recent price cuts of roughly $8,000 across the range have sharpened its position against cheaper Chinese EVs without changing the fundamental verdict: a sound, unexciting choice rather than a class leader.
pros: Spacious, well-packaged interior for the class, with strong rear legroom and a rare space-saver spare wheel
Comfortable, well-damped ride that soaks up potholes and speed bumps around town
Easy-to-use dual-screen infotainment with thoughtful right-hand-drive ergonomics
Extended Range grade seen by reviewers as strong value following 2026 price cuts, undercutting the Premium by around $10,000 for similar underlying capability
cons: Standard Range's real-world range (around 350km) looks light for a modern EV, especially for interstate trips
100kW DC fast-charging trails newer 800V rivals and is described by reviewers as not great for the segment
Chassis gets bouncy and less composed at highway speed or when pushed harder
Premium trim's price premium over Extended Range is questioned as not clearly justified by the added equipment

summary: Kia's compact electric SUV pairs a genuinely spacious, well-finished cabin with suspension tuning that Australian reviewers rate as composed and comfortable over rough surfaces. Entry Air variants are seen as strong value under $50k with usable real-world range, but the flagship GT-Line drifts close to $70,000 on-road, where reviewers feel it should offer more standard safety kit such as a surround-view camera.
pros: Locally tuned ride soaks up broken Melbourne road surfaces while staying composed at highway speed
Roomy, well-packaged cabin and a genuinely usable 460L boot (1250L seats folded) for a compact SUV
Air Long Range offers a genuinely long 604km WLTP claim while still pricing under $55,000
Five-star ANCAP rating and Kia's 7-year/unlimited-km vehicle warranty (7yr/150,000km battery)
cons: GT-Line pricing approaches $70,000 drive-away yet still lacks a surround-view camera
Noticeable road and wind noise intrude at highway speeds on all variants
Modest DC fast-charging speeds mean longer top-up stops on road trips than key rivals
Entry Air Standard Range is rated to tow just 500kg braked, well below the 1000kg of Long Range variants

summary: Roomy mid-size electric SUV with a huge boot and Kia's class-leading 7-year warranty, priced to undercut most mid-size EV rivals.
pros: Largest boot in this comparison at 513L (1714L seats down)
7-year/150,000km vehicle and battery warranty
Comfortable, family-friendly interior with strong rear-seat space
cons: Entry Air Standard Range is front-wheel drive only and rated to tow just 300kg braked
DC charging tops out lower than rivals, so road-trip top-ups take longer
Firmer low-speed ride than some competitors on Melbourne's rougher back streets

summary: The facelifted 2026 Kia EV6 remains one of the most engaging mid-size electric SUVs to drive, with Australian reviewers rating its handling and steering among the best of any EV regardless of price, backed by rapid 800V DC charging and a now-uniform 84kWh battery that lifts range across every grade. It reads more as an electric grand tourer than a family hauler, though: reviewers consistently flag a smaller-than-expected boot, tight rear headroom and a busy low-speed ride, and note the range is priced at a premium against newer rivals, with the flagship GT landing well clear of the top FBT exemption threshold.
pros: Genuinely excellent handling and steering feel, rated by multiple reviewers among the best-driving EVs at any price
800V architecture enables very fast DC charging, around 10-80% in 18 minutes
Larger 84kWh battery lifts WLTP range across the range, up to 582km on the entry Air RWD
Strong 7-year/unlimited-km vehicle warranty with 7-year/150,000km high-voltage battery cover
cons: 480L boot trails key rivals such as the Ford Mustang Mach-E despite premium pricing
Tight rear headroom and harder rear-seat plastics let down an otherwise upmarket cabin
Speed-limit and driver-attention warnings are persistent and reset every drive
Priced above many rivals, with GT-Line and GT grades pushing well past the $75,000 FBT threshold and the GT AWD clearing $91,661 outright

summary: Kia's flagship seven-seat electric SUV is consistently praised by Australian reviewers as one of the most family-practical EVs on sale, with a genuinely usable third row, fast 800V DC charging, and a plush, tech-laden cabin. It comes at a real cost though, with even the entry Air RWD pricing above the luxury-EV threshold and the range topping out with the performance-focused GT, which reviewers see more as a halo model than a value pick.
pros: Spacious, genuinely adult-friendly third row that few seven-seat EV rivals match
Fast 800V architecture supports rapid DC charging, useful for family road trips
High-quality, feature-rich interior with strong safety tech across the range
Strong 7-year/unlimited-km warranty backing the whole lineup
cons: Every variant is priced above the FBT exemption threshold, eroding novated lease appeal
Big and heavy, so real-world efficiency and around-town manoeuvrability suffer versus smaller EVs
Boot space behind the third row is tight when all seven seats are needed
GT flagship commands a large premium mainly for extra performance few buyers will use

summary: The EQA is Mercedes-Benz's entry-level electric SUV, essentially a battery-electric GLA with a front-mounted motor and the brand's usual small-SUV proportions. Australian reviewers consistently praise its refined, adaptive-damper ride and slick MBUX cabin, but mark it down for a WLTP range and boot space that trail cheaper, more spacious rivals now on sale locally. It reads as a car for buyers who want three-pointed-star badge appeal and a comfortable, quiet cabin rather than the last word in efficiency or outright value.
pros: Refined, well-damped ride quality even on larger wheels, reviewers say it feels bigger than its footprint
Smooth, linear power delivery from the single front motor makes it easy and relaxing to drive in town
Upscale MBUX cabin with twin 10.25-inch displays and quality materials typical of the brand
Now priced under the luxury car tax threshold across the range, helped by repeated local price cuts
cons: Reviewers note numerous rivals offer better range and/or value for similar or less money
Compromised rear legroom and a smaller-than-expected boot due to battery packaging
Divisive EQ-era styling elements, some reviewers say the design is starting to look dated
WLTP range and real-world efficiency trail newer competitors despite the premium price

summary: The MG4 is consistently rated by Australian reviewers as one of the best-value small EVs on sale, combining sharp pricing with genuinely engaging rear-wheel-drive handling that punches above its budget-hatch positioning. The 2026 update fixed earlier interior gripes (better seats, more responsive touchscreen) and added the entry-level Urban variant, which reviewers praise for segment-busting cabin space and a surprisingly mature ride for the money. Common criticisms are a fiddly climate interface, an overactive speed-limit warning chime, and a boot that's merely adequate rather than class-leading.
pros: Sharp pricing relative to range and equipment, undercutting most EV rivals
Engaging, well-sorted rear-wheel-drive handling and steering feel
Spacious, upmarket-feeling cabin for the price, especially in Urban trim
Strong standard safety suite (adaptive cruise, AEB, blind spot monitoring)
Quick DC charging (10-80% in around 25-30 minutes)
cons: Boot space is only middling for a hatch (350-382L)
Few physical controls; climate functions buried in the touchscreen
Overactive speed-limit and driver-attention warning chimes annoy some reviewers
XPower's real-world range drops noticeably under highway/AWD use

summary: The Polestar 4 is a coupe-styled mid-size electric SUV that Australian reviewers rate highly for its involving, well-composed driving manners, spacious and upmarket cabin, and genuinely competitive pricing against premium rivals like the Porsche Macan Electric. Its standout talking point is the deletion of a conventional rear window in favour of a camera-fed digital mirror, a decision reviewers describe as a workable, even class-leading, trade for headroom but not a universally comfortable one. Value is undercut by a lengthy, pricey options list and a control layout that pushes nearly everything through the touchscreen.
pros: Involving, well-controlled ride and handling that belies the car's size, with the Single Motor judged the best-balanced everyday pick
Spacious, near-limo-like rear seat and a large, usefully square 526-litre boot
Classy, well-finished interior with a crisp 15.4-inch Android Automotive infotainment system
Strong ownership package: 5-year/100,000km free servicing and 5-year unlimited-kilometre warranty
Undercuts key premium EV rivals such as the Porsche Macan Electric on price
cons: No rear window: the camera-fed digital mirror lacks the depth perception of a real mirror, and at least one reviewer reported a passenger became carsick watching the live feed

Near-total reliance on the touchscreen and touch-sensitive steering wheel controls for basic functions like mirrors, seat heating and cruise control fine-adjustment, which reviewers flagged as fiddly and distracting
Lengthy, expensive options list (Plus Pack, Pro Pack, Nappa leather) means the well-equipped price climbs well past the base figure
DC fast-charging speed is competent but trails class-leading rivals
Polestar's smaller Australian dealer and service footprint compared to established luxury brands

summary: Australian reviewers regard the updated Model 3 as the class benchmark among electric sedans, praising a noticeably quieter cabin and softer ride than earlier versions alongside brisk performance and strong efficiency. The Long Range RWD's 750km WLTP claim makes it the longest-range EV sold in the country, while the screen-only control layout continues to split opinion. The Performance variant's near-$81,000 list price also pushes it close to the FBT exemption threshold that keeps novated-lease buyers interested in the cheaper variants.
pros: Long Range RWD offers the longest WLTP range of any EV on sale in Australia at 750km
Access to Tesla's extensive Australian Supercharger network plus regular over-the-air software updates
Recent refresh brings a quieter cabin and noticeably improved ride comfort over the outgoing model
Strong outright performance, with the dual-motor Performance variant hitting 100km/h in around 3.1 seconds
cons: Touchscreen-only interface, including indicators and gear selection on some builds, remains a sticking point for reviewers
Comprehensive insurance premiums tend to sit at the higher end of the EV market due to repair and parts costs
Performance variant's list price sits close to the $75,000 FBT exemption threshold, eroding some of the novated-lease tax advantage

summary: Best-selling electric SUV globally, offering the longest range and lowest energy use of this trio plus access to Tesla's Supercharger network.
pros: Longest range in this comparison at 466km WLTP
Most efficient of the three at 13.9kWh/100km, lowering running costs
Direct access to Tesla's extensive Australian Supercharger network and frequent over-the-air updates
cons: Touchscreen-only controls, including for indicators and gear selection on some builds, split opinion
Comprehensive insurance premiums tend to run higher than the Kia or BYD due to repair costs
Braked towing capacity on the RWD variant is lower than the AWD Model Y variants

summary: The EX30 is Volvo's compact electric SUV, praised by Australian reviewers for punchy, agile handling, a well-damped ride and a distinctive, upmarket cabin featuring wool-blend seat trim. Sharp price cuts through 2026 have pushed the single-motor Plus below $50,000 before on-roads, making it one of the more attainable premium-badged EVs on the market, and it carries a five-star ANCAP safety rating. It is let down for family duty by a tight rear seat and modest boot, and reviewers are split on whether that's a fair trade-off for its style and driving manners.
pros: Agile, well-controlled handling and a comfortable ride, with brisk acceleration even in the base single-motor form
Distinctive Scandinavian interior design with higher-grade materials, including wool-blend seat trim, that feels a step above rivals
Aggressive 2026 price cuts (Plus from $49,990 before on-roads) bring a premium-badged EV within reach of mainstream buyers
Five-star ANCAP safety rating and strong standard safety tech
cons: Almost every function -- climate control, mirror adjustment, even the glovebox -- is buried in the portrait touchscreen with no driver instrument display; some reviewers call this the car's biggest flaw and report the screen lagging or crashing, while others say it becomes tolerable after a week of familiarity, so opinion is genuinely split rather than uniformly negative
Window switches are relocated to the centre console instead of the doors, one of several cost-saving control choices reviewers find awkward
Small rear seat and boot space limit its practicality as a family car
DC fast-charging speeds are competent rather than class-leading

summary: The XPeng G6 is a mid-size electric SUV coupe pitched squarely at the Tesla Model Y, with reviewers praising its upmarket cabin, strong tech package and genuinely quick charging on the refreshed 800V architecture. Testers rate the ride and refinement highly and note the flagship AWD Performance model undercuts a comparable Model Y on price while offering vastly stronger acceleration. The main knocks are steering that feels heavy and artificial, a chassis that doesn't quite match the Performance variant's straight-line pace, and quirks like the lack of a glovebox and a fiddly steering-column gear selector.
pros: Upmarket interior fit-out and strong tech/safety suite for the price
Fast 800V/451kW DC charging with a 10-80% top-up around 12 minutes
AWD Performance variant offers Tesla Model Y Performance-rivalling pace at a lower price
Spacious rear seating with good headroom for a coupe-SUV shape
cons: Steering feels heavy and artificial, chassis doesn't fully back up the Performance model's speed
No glovebox and limited cabin storage
Counterintuitive steering-column gear selector
Newer brand with a history of distributor changes in Australia, which may concern some buyers on parts/service continuity
